newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FEATURE - Kazakh Uighurs welcome freedom in cold bleak town.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kazakh Uighurs welcome freedom in cold bleak town.

text.p: Living conditions are harsh in this town lost in the vast Kazakh steppe. But many local residents -- ethnic Uighurs -- say they are happy because they have more freedom than their ethnic kin in nearby China.

Zharkent, a windswept town with a population of more than 50,000 some 300 km (190 miles) east of the Kazakh capital Almaty and 30 km (18 miles) from the Chinese border, has had no electricity, heating or warm water since last August.
The town, whose residents' monthly salaries average a mere $50, simply cannot afford to pay for electricity and heating bought in neighbouring regions of the country.

Candles -- brought from China and Russia -- are the most profitable merchandise. The price often goes up at night when the town plunges into darkness. Some shops are lit with precious family heirlooms -- kerosene lamps inherited from grandparents.
The local brewery, winery and a concrete factory are at a standstill. Only a huge market selling cheap merchandise from neighbouring China which allows the town to survive.

But while they are happy to trade with China, where their ancestors -- nomadic Moslem Turkic tribes -- originally settled, the Uighurs who make up 40 percent of Zharkent's population have no desire to go back over the border to live.
UIGHURS FLED DISCRIMINATION FROM CHINESE
Turlygodzha Kurbanov, a local ethnic Uighur, was five when his parents found refuge in the then-Soviet republic of Kazakhstan in 1962.
"My parents fled from China because they were Uighurs and were treated as second rate. Life is not easy in Kazakhstan but there is no discrimination here," Kurbanov says.
Earlier this month, China's northern Xinjiang province was shaken by a huge anti-Chinese riot by local Uighurs.
Beijing said it started after an Uighur criminal suspect resisted arrest by police.

Leaders of an exiled nationalist Uighur group said the disturbances had been triggered by "China's colonial policy, genocide, mass influx of ethnic Han Chinese and social economic problems of the Uighurs".
Chinese officials said nine people were killed in clashes with the army and the police. Uighur leaders say at least 80 died.
The riot was one of the largest and most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.
News about it travelled fast to Kazakhstan.

"Uighurs in China have been driven to despair by discrimination and have no alternative but to riot...I heard that Uighurs disappear overnight in China if they are not loyal to the authorities," Kurbanov said.

Not every Uighur in Kazakhstan has the same spacious house, as Kurbanov, a successful businessman thriving largely on border trade with China whose home has pheasants in the inner yard and tables groaning with food. But most say they can freely develop their culture here and speak their native language.
"We are very grateful to the Kazakh government and people for their hospitality," said Kurvanbuvi Ashimova, an activist from the local Uighur cultural society.
KAZAKHS PUT GOOD NEIGHBOURLINESS ABOVE SEPARATIST CALLS
More than 300,000 Uighurs live in the former Soviet Union, and some 180,000 in Kazakhstan alone.
China says that seven to nine million Uighurs live there, mostly in Xinjiang province, while Uighurs put the figure at some 20 million people.

In the 1930's many Uighurs fled to China to escape repression under Soviet dictator Josef Stalin. Thirty years later the human flood turned back the other way due to discrimination by ethnic Han Chinese.
Makhmud Islamov, himself an ethnic Uighur, was in charge of a special commission on the resettlement of Uighurs back to the Soviet Union.
"The main influx of Turkic refugees (from China) -- Uighurs, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz -- was in 1962. That year alone, we resettled 150,000 refugees," Islamov said.
He admits that living standards in China have risen considerably over the last 30 years but says the human rights situation there has not improved.
"Today the Chinese treat smaller nationalities no better than 30 years ago, and if you are an Uighur you can't be even a taxi driver in China," he said.
Calls often heard from exiled Uighur leaders to create a national state in northern China seem to be finding backing among Uighurs living densely in southeastern Kazakhstan.
"China will never give up our lands rich in oil and metals. But we hope all Uighurs will be united anyway," Kurbanov said.
"History says that lands in northern China are ours...Maybe, the Chinese will give us our land back?" Ashimova said.

But Adylshaiyk Ibraimoldayev, head of the local administration and an ethnic Kazakh, thinks that the Uighurs' calls for independence are doomed and that Kazakhstan's ties of good-neighbourliness with China will not be disturbed by separatist calls.
"Has China ever recognised separatist states? It will just say its firm 'no', and that's that," Ibraimoldayev said.
